### `psych`

The `psych` package [@revelle_2024]  includes MANY functions that help with data exploration and running analyses typically done in the social sciences. It is particluarly useful for exploratory factor analyses. 

### `carData`

The `carData` package [@fox_etal_2022] contains many datasets. Most of these datasets are used in the book titled *an R Companion to Applied Regression*.

:::

:::

::: {.column width = '50%'}
<center style="padding-bottom: 21px;"> [Data]{.data-title} </center>

Today we will work with the `prestige` dataset. This dataset contains the perceived prestige and other variables related to 102 professions in Canada in 1971.
 
```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true 
#| message: false
#| code-line-numbers: false
#| classes: code-125

dat <- carData::Prestige
```

                                 desc =  labels,

                     style = list(fontFamily = "Work Sans, sans-serif", fontSize = ".9rem"),

::::


## Association Between Variables

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width = '30%'}

When look at scatterplots, we can intuitively spot *associations between two variables*. 


::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}

If we plot `eduaction` and `prestige`, we can tell that there is some sort of **trend**; as the values of one variable increase, the values of the other variable also increase. 
:::


::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}

<center style="font-size:32px"> In simple terms, both correlation and regression provide some *numerical summaries* of these trends/associations. 
</center>

:::



:::
::: {.column width = '70%'}

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true 
#| out-width: "100%"
#| code-line-numbers: false
#| classes: code-125


ggplot(data = dat,
        aes(x = education, y = prestige)) +
          geom_point()
```


:::
::::


## Covariance

The most basic measure of association between two continuous cariables is the **covariance**. The *sign* of the covaraince describes the *direction* of the relation between two variables:


:::: {.panel-tabset}

### Positive Covariance

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width = '50%'}
```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true 
#| out-width: "100%"
#| code-line-numbers: false
#| classes: code-125


ggplot(data = dat,
        aes(x = education, y = prestige)) +
          geom_point()
```


:::
::: {.column width = '50%'}

We can use `cov()` to calculate the covariance between `education` and `prestige`:

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true 
#| code-line-numbers: false
#| classes: code-125

cov(dat$education, dat$prestige)
```


The covariance is positive so we know that as one variable increases or decreases, so does the other variable. In this case, the higher the average years of `education` of individuals in a profession, the higher the perceived `prestige` of that profession.


:::
::::

### Negative Covaraince

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width = '50%'}
```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true 
#| out-width: "100%"
#| code-line-numbers: false
#| classes: code-125


ggplot(data = dat,
        aes(x = women, y = income)) +
          geom_point()
```


:::
::: {.column width = '50%'}

If we calculate the covariance between `women` and `income`:

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true 
#| code-line-numbers: false
#| classes: code-125

cov(dat$women, dat$income)
```


We see that the covariance is negative. meaning that, in 1971, the more women were in a certain profession, the less was the average income for that profession.

:::
::::

::::



## When Comparisons are meaningless



On the previous slide we say that the first covariance was around $39.9$ and the second covariance was around $-59411.38$. Does this mean that the second relationship is much stronger than the first one? Absolutely not. The values of covariances cannot be compared when variables are measured on *different scales*. The formula for the covariance is:

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
$$S_{xy} = \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x}) \times (y_i - \bar{y})}{n - 1}$$

:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width = '50%'}

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}

The raw covariance values are meaningless because the `income` variable is measured on a scale that is much larger than either `education` or `prestige`.

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true 
#| code-line-numbers: false
#| classes: code-125

# Range of 3 variables. apply() functions apply the same function to multiple columns/rows of a matrix
apply(dat[,1:3], 2, range)
```

:::

:::
::: {.column width = '50%'}

::: {.fragment fragment-index=3}

If you look at the formula for $S_{xy}$, when `income` is involved, you can expect the result to be quite large. 


Asking which covariance is larger is essentially the same as asking whether 84 degrees Fahrenheit is larger than 30 degrees Celsius. 

:::


::: {.fragment fragment-index=4}
Actually what would you do to answer the question in the line above? 🤔
:::


:::
::::


## Changing Variable Scales: Standardization


::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}

To compare measurements on different scales (Fahrenheit VS Celsius), we need to *transform* one of them, such that they are on the *same scale*. We have briefly talked about *Z-scores* in [Lab 4](https://fabio-setti.netlify.app/psyc6802/lab_4#/outliers-standardized-units){target='_blank'}. Turning variables into Z-scores is known as **standardizing** and it is just a convenient way of rescaling variables such that they are all on the same scale. For any variable $X$:

$$z_i = \frac{x_i - \bar{x}}{S_x}$$

:::


:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width = '50%'}

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}

we can standardize variables with the `scale()` function:

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true 
#| code-line-numbers: false
#| classes: code-125

# here I am adding the standardized variable to the dataset
dat$education_std <- scale(dat$education)[,1]
```

**NOTE:** remember to always add the `[,1]` when using the `scale()` function. Try running `scale(dat$education)` and look at the output.

:::

:::
::: {.column width = '50%'}

::: {.fragment fragment-index=3}

Any standardized variable will have mean = 0 and sd (or variance) = 1:

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true 
#| code-line-numbers: false
#| classes: code-125

mean(dat$education_std)
sd(dat$education_std)
```

:::

:::
::::


## The Steps Graphically

The important point is that standardizing does not change the shape of the distribution of a variable, it just moves it and resizes it. let's look at what happens step by step when we standardize `education`:

:::: {.panel-tabset}

### Original Distribution

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width = '70%'}
```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true 
#| code-line-numbers: false
#| classes: code-125
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Plot Code"

ggplot(dat, aes(x = education)) +
  geom_density(aes(color = "Raw")) +
  xlim(c(-10, 20)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0,0)) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("Raw" = "blue"),
    name = "",
    labels = c( "Raw" = expression(x[i]))) +
  theme(
    axis.title.y = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y  = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),
    axis.line.y  = element_blank())
```


:::
::: {.column width = '30%'}

The blue density is the original `education` variable and it represents the average years of education for each of the 102 occupations in the data.

This is the $x_i$ part of the formula

$$z_i = \frac{x_i - \bar{x}}{S_x}$$


:::
::::


### Subtract the Mean

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width = '70%'}
```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true 
#| code-line-numbers: false
#| classes: code-125
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Plot Code"

ggplot(dat, aes(x = education)) +
  geom_density(aes(color = "Raw")) +
  geom_density(aes(x = education - mean(dat$education), color = "Centered")) +
  xlim(c(-10, 20)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0,0)) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("Raw" = "blue",
               "Centered" = "red"),
    name = "",
    labels = c(
      "Raw" = expression(x[i]),
      "Centered" = expression(x[i] - bar(x)))) +
  theme(
    axis.title.y = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y  = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),
    axis.line.y  = element_blank())

```


:::
::: {.column width = '30%'}

The red density is the `education` variable after we subtract its mean from all the values. So the red density represents the the $x_i - \bar{x}$ part of $z_i = \frac{x_i - \bar{x}}{S_x}$. 


This is known as **mean centering**, and it comes up in moderation anlyses to get easier interpretations. 

:::
::::




### Divide By the SD


:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width = '65%'}
```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true 
#| code-line-numbers: false
#| classes: code-125
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Plot Code"

ggplot(dat, aes(x = education)) +
  geom_density(aes(color = "Raw")) +
  geom_density(aes(x = education - mean(dat$education), color = "Centered")) +
  geom_density(aes(x = (education - mean(dat$education)) / sd(dat$education),
                   color = "Standardized")) +
  xlim(c(-10, 20)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0,0)) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("Raw" = "blue",
               "Centered" = "red",
               "Standardized" = "purple"),
    name = "",
    labels = c(
      "Raw" = expression(x[i]),
      "Centered" = expression(x[i] - bar(x)),
      "Standardized" = expression((x[i] - bar(x)) / S[x])
    )
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.title.y = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y  = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),
    axis.line.y  = element_blank())
```


:::
::: {.column width = '35%'}

The purple density is $z_i = \frac{x_i - \bar{x}}{S_x}$. Dividing by the SD "squishes" the distribution, but the shape does not change! The important implication is that standardizing *does not change the relation* between variables. 


<p style='font-size: 22px'> Note that there is nothing special about mean = 0 and SD = 1. You could add any value and that will become the new mean. Having a mean of 0 and an SD of 1 usually makes things easier. </p>



:::
::::

::::


## Covariance With standardized Variables?

Let's standardize the variables from before, compute the covariance again and see what happens:
```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true 
#| code-line-numbers: false
#| classes: code-125

dat$education_std <- scale(dat$education)[,1]
dat$prestige_std <- scale(dat$prestige)[,1]
dat$women_std <- scale(dat$women)[,1]
dat$income_std <- scale(dat$income)[,1]
```


:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width = '50%'}


::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}

With the original variables we got:

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true 
#| code-line-numbers: false
#| classes: code-125

cov(dat$education, dat$prestige)
cov(dat$women, dat$income)
```

:::

:::
::: {.column width = '50%'}


::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
With the standardized variables, we get:

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true 
#| code-line-numbers: false
#| classes: code-125

cov(dat$education_std, dat$prestige_std)
cov(dat$women_std, dat$income_std)
```

:::

:::
::::


::: {.fragment fragment-index=3}
While originally the covariance between `women` and `income` had a much larger number, once the variables are standardized, the relation between `education` and `prestige` has the larger number. 
:::


::: {.fragment fragment-index=4}
The numbers in the right column are the **correlation coefficient** between the variables and are definitely what we should look at when determining how strong a relation is.
:::


## It was the Correlation all Along

You don't hear about covariance very often because it is not interpretable, as its value depend on the scale of the original variables. The **correlation**, denoted with $r$, is the <u>standardized covariance</u> and has the benefit of always being between -1 and 1. 

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width = '50%'}


::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}

we can compute the correlation between two variables with the `cor()` function:

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true 
#| code-line-numbers: false
#| classes: code-125

# We use the original variables because they are standardized within the correlation formula. The steps from before were only intended to demonstrate the equivalence between correaltion and covariance
cor(dat$education, dat$prestige)
cor(dat$women, dat$income)
```

:::

:::
::: {.column width = '50%'}

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}

- $r = 0$: a correlation of 0 exactly means that there is *no linear association* between two variables.

- $r > 0$: a correlation above 0 means that there is a *positive linear association* between two variables.  

- $r < 0$: a correlation below 0 means that there is a *negative linear association* between two variables. 

:::

:::
::::


::: {.fragment fragment-index=3}
So, there is a strong positive relation between `education` need for a certain occupation and the perceived `prestige` of that occupation. 
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=4}
Likewise, there is a fairly noticeable negative relation between the average `income` by profession and the percentage of women practicing that profession.
:::

## Significance Test for Correlation

The `cor()` function does not provide any *p*-value. We need to use the `corTest()` function from the `psych` package for that. Here is the example for the correaltion between `education` and `prestige`:

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width = '50%'}

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true 
#| code-line-numbers: false
#| classes: code-125

psych::corTest(dat$education, dat$prestige)
```

:::

:::
::: {.column width = '50%'}

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
Lots of text! But if we take a closer look it should be fairly straightforward:

- The correlation, $r = .85$, is below the `Correlation matrix` line.

- The sample size, $n = 102$, is also returned.

- The *p*-value is the last number displayed. Here it's so small that the function just rounds to 0, so, $p < .001$.

:::

:::
::::

</br>

::: {.fragment fragment-index=3}

The last line of the output tells us that if we want the 95\% CI for the correlation coefficient, we can get that by adding the `short=FALSE` argument to the `corTest()` function.

:::

## Correlation matrices

Correlation matrices are  square tables that summarize the correlation between a set of variables. 

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width = '50%'}

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}

Here is the correlation matrix among the first 4 variables in the the data:

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true 
#| code-line-numbers: false
#| classes: code-125

cor(dat[,1:4])
```

Each cell is the correlation between the variables in the row and column. Notice that the matrix is *symmetric*, meaning that the values in the top and bottom triangle are the same. This is because $\mathrm{cor(x, y)} = \mathrm{cor(y, x)}$. 

Why would the diagonal be all 1s?

:::


:::

::: {.column width = '50%'}


::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}

You can get the equivalent with the `corTest()` function, but I suggest you do this:

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true 
#| code-line-numbers: false
#| classes: code-125

cor_mat <- corTest(dat[,1:4])
cor_mat$r
```


Notice how we are extracrting the `r` element from the `cor_mat` object that we created. The `r` element is the correlation matrix, but there's much more information inside `cor_mat`. 

:::

:::
::::

## Contents of `cor.test()`

When reporting results you will usually need to also report the significance tests (see this slide N for APA style resources) and other information. Let's look at the names of the elements inside `cor_mat`:

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true 
#| code-line-numbers: false
#| classes: code-125

names(cor_mat)
```


:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width = '50%'}

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}

The `ci` element gives a neater output and also the CIs and *p*-values!

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true 
#| code-line-numbers: false
#| classes: code-125

round(cor_mat$ci, digits = 3)
```

:::

:::
::: {.column width = '50%'}

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
the `t` element are the *t*-statistics associated with all the correlations:

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true 
#| code-line-numbers: false
#| classes: code-125

round(cor_mat$t, digits = 2)
```

:::

:::
::::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=3}
To find out what all the elements are, look under the **value** section of the `corTest()` help menu.
:::

## Point-Bisedrial Correlation {visibility="hidden"}

Correlation should only be used to measure the association between continuous variables. What to do if one variable is dichotomous and the other is continuous? We can use the **point-biserial correlation**. 

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width = '50%'}

We need a *dichotomous* variable (i.e., only two categories). For the sake of the example, let's filter the data such that we only have `bc` and `wc` for the `type` variable

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true 
#| code-line-numbers: false
#| classes: code-125

# wc and bc stand for blue collar and white collar
dat_filt <- dat %>% 
             filter(type %in% c("wc", "bc"))

table(dat_filt$type)
```

So now we are only left with blue collar and white collar jobs.

:::
::: {.column width = '50%'}

What is the relation between `type` and `income`? We can use the `biserial()` function from the `psych` package to calculate the point-biserial correlation:

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true 
#| code-line-numbers: false
#| classes: code-125

psych::biserial(dat_filt$income, 
                dat_filt$type)
```

Surprisingly, there isn's that much of a relation between job type and income (although we are comparing only white collar and blue collar jobs)

:::
::::


## Linear Regression

Onto what is probably the most important analysis in statistics, **linear regression**. On slide 2 we showed the scatterplot between `education` and `prestige`, and saw a noticeable trend.


:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width = '40%'}

A *regression line* capture the linear trend between two variables.

More importantly, the regression line has a very simple mathematical form, 

$$y = b_0 + b_1 \times x$$

In the case of this graph, we would write: 

$$\mathrm{prestige} = b_0 + b_1 \times \mathrm{education}$$


meaning that we think that perceived occupation `prestige` is *predicted* by the `education` required for that occupation.

:::
::: {.column width = '60%'}

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true 
#| code-line-numbers: false
#| classes: code-125
ggplot(data = dat,
        aes(x = education, y = prestige)) +
          geom_point() +
           geom_smooth(method = "lm")
```

:::
::::

## Running a Regression in `R`

We can run a regression in `R` by using the `lm()` function (stand for *linear model*). Let's run a regression with `education` predicting `prestige`:

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width = '55%'}

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true 
#| code-line-numbers: false
#| classes: code-125

reg <- lm(prestige ~ education, dat = dat)
summary(reg)
```

:::
::: {.column width = '45%'}

we use the `summary()` function to get a summary of the results of an `lm` object. A quick overview of the output:

<ul style='font-size: 26px'>

<li> `call:` this is just the function formula. </li>

<li> `Residuals:` this gives a quick summary of the distribution of the *residuals*. (more on residuals later) </li>

<li> `coefficients:` this is where you find the regression coefficients along with their significance test. </li>

<li> The last part contains the $R^2$, which is a measure of how good the regression predicts the $y$ variable. </li>

</ul>


:::
::::


## The Coefficients

The syntax for `lm()` is the same that we used for the independent samples *t*-test. `prestige ~ education` is saying "predict `prestige` with `education`". The we have to specify the data where the variables come from with `data =`. 

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width = '55%'}

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true 
#| code-line-numbers: false
#| classes: code-125

reg <- lm(prestige ~ education, dat = dat)
summary(reg)
```

:::
::: {.column width = '45%'}

our regression coffiecents are $b_0$ and $b_1$.

<ul style='font-size: 24px'>

<li> $b_0 = -10.73$, the *intercept*:  The *expected value* of `prestige` when `education` is 0. You may notice that that `prestige` cannot ever be below 0, so this should be impossible in practice (see next slide). </li>

<li> $b_1 = 5.36$, the *slope*: The *expected change* in `prestige` per 1-unit increase in `education`.  </li>

</ul>

The regression equation is 

$$\mathrm{prestige} = -10.73 + 5.36 \times \mathrm{education}$$

:::
::::

## Regression Coefficients: Intercept

The intercept, $b_0$, is the "expected value of the $y$ variable when $x$ is 0". In our case, $b_0 = -10.73$. This number makes no sense for two reasons: *(1)* `prestige` cannot be negative, and *(2)* `education` cannot be 0. What is going on? 🤨


:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width = '40%'}

The intercept is mathematically where the regression line hits the $y$-axis. If the the 0 value for $x$ is out of range, than the intercept will generally be meaningless.

This is not an "issue" and it's only a consequence of the *scale* of our variables. We will see what happens once we standardize our variables.

In practice, you do not care much about the intercept, as it does not carry any information about the relation between the $x$ and $y$ variables.

:::
::: {.column width = '60%'}

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true 
#| code-line-numbers: false
#| classes: code-125
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Plot Code"


ggplot(data = dat,
        aes(x = education, y = prestige)) +
          geom_point() +
            geom_abline(intercept =  as.numeric(reg$coefficients[1]), 
                        slope =  as.numeric(reg$coefficients[2], 
                        fill = "#7a0b80"))+
             geom_vline(xintercept = 0, lty = 2) +
             geom_segment(y = as.numeric(reg$coefficients[1]), x = 0,
                          yend = as.numeric(reg$coefficients[1]), xend = -10, lty = 3) +
            annotate("text", x = -3, y = 0, label = "the dot is the \n intercept") +
            geom_point(aes(x = 0, y = as.numeric(reg$coefficients[1]), col = "red", size = 3), show.legend = FALSE) +
             xlim(c(-5, 20)) +
             ylim(c(-30, 90))

```

:::
::::

## Regression Coefficients: Slope

The slope, $b_1$, is the "expected change in the $y$ variable for each 1-unit change in the $x$ variable". In our case, $b_1 = 5.36$. This sounds much harder than it is in practice. Given the equation
$$\mathrm{prestige} = -10.73 + 5.36 \times \mathrm{education}$$

We can plug in some values for `education` and get the *predicted value* for `prestige`. 


:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width = '50%'}

- if $\mathrm{education} = 1$, then $\mathrm{prestige} = -10.73 + 5.36 \times 1 = -5.37$


- if $\mathrm{education} = 2$, then $\mathrm{prestige} = -10.73 + 5.36 \times 2 = -0.01$


- if $\mathrm{education} = 10$, then $\mathrm{prestige} = -10.73 + 5.36 \times 10 = 42.87$

:::


::: {.column width = '50%'}

the "1-unit change" part comes from the $5.36 \times \mathrm{education}$ term in the regression equation. 

As you change `education` by 1, `prestige` changes by $5.36$ times that. If you change `education` by 2-units, then `prestige` changes by $10.72$.
:::
::::

Note that the *sign* of the slope tells you whether two variables are positively or negatively related. As we already saw with the correlation, `prestige` and `education` are positively related.


## More Slopes Examples

It follows that the sign of the slope determines whether the line trends up (positive slope) or down (negative slope). Here are some examples:


:::: {.panel-tabset}

### Positive Relation

::: {.column width = '70%'}

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true 
#| code-line-numbers: false
#| classes: code-125
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "plot Code"

ggplot(data = dat,
        aes(x = education, y = prestige)) +
          geom_point() +
          geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)
```


:::
::: {.column width = '30%'}

Correlation:

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true 
#| code-line-numbers: false
#| classes: code-125


cor(dat$prestige, dat$education)
```




Slope:
```{r}
#| eval: true

lm(prestige ~ education, data = dat)$coef[2]
```

## Regression With stndardized Variables

Let's look at what happens when we run a regression with the same variables, but standardized. What is the same and what is different? 

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width = '50%'}

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true 
#| code-line-numbers: false
#| classes: code-125

reg <- lm(prestige ~ education, dat = dat)
summary(reg)
```


:::
::: {.column width = '50%'}


```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true 
#| code-line-numbers: false
#| classes: code-125

reg_std <- lm(prestige_std ~ education_std, dat = dat)
summary(reg_std)
```

:::
::::

:::

::: {.column width = '50%'}

## Standardized Coefficients: Intercept

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width = '30%'}

Whenever we standardize all the variables in a regression, the intercept will always be 0.

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true 
#| code-line-numbers: false
#| classes: code-125

round(reg_std$coef[1], 3)
```

This is because standardizing has the effect of centering the data, and the regression line, at the 0 point. 


This is apparent in the graph on the right, where the regression line hits the *y*-axis at 0 exactly.

:::
::: {.column width = '70%'}
```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true 
#| code-line-numbers: false
#| out-width: "110%"
#| classes: code-125
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Plot Code"

ggplot(data = dat,
        aes(x = education_std, y = prestige_std)) +
          geom_point() +
          geom_hline(yintercept = 0, lty = 3) +
          geom_vline(xintercept = 0, lty = 3) +
          geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)
```

:::
::::


## Standardized Coefficients: Slope

In the case of a regression with two variables, the standardized regression slope <u>is the correlation coefficient</u>. As a reminder, here are the unstandardized regression coefficient, standardized regression coefficient, and correlation between `prestige` and `education`:


:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width = '40%'}

Unstandardized regression:

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true 
#| code-line-numbers: false
#| classes: code-115

round(summary(reg)$coefficients, 2)
```

:::

::: {.column width = '40%'}

Standardized regression:

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true 
#| code-line-numbers: false
#| classes: code-115

round(summary(reg_std)$coefficients, 2)
```

:::

::: {.column width = '20%'}

Correlation:

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true 
#| code-line-numbers: false
#| classes: code-125

round(cor_mat$r[4,1], 2)

# t-statistic for correlation
round(cor_mat$t[4,1], 2)
```

:::
::::



Notice that the standardized regression coefficient and and the correlation are both $0.85$. The unstandardized regression coefficient is different although 


Additionally, I made sure to print the $t$-values associated with the 3 statistics above. I want to emphasize that the $t$-values are the exact same in all 3 cases 🤔



## If the $t$-statistic is the same...

To refer back to hypothesis testing, we use test statistics like the $t$-statistic to test hypotheses. In the case of regression and correlation, the $t$-statistic is always used to ask this question:

<center style:"font-size: 30px;"> <u>Is the relation between two variables significantly different from 0?</u> </center>

Then, if the $t$-statistics are the exact same, it means that we are asking the same exact question. In other words, unstandardized, standardized regression coefficients, and correlations are one and the same. 

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width = '50%'}

<center> 

The *true temperature* does not change whether we measure it in Fahrenheit or Celsius; similarly, the true relation between two variables does not depend on the numbers we choose to represent those variables. 🧘

</center>


It may not click now, but *why* this point is very important will become clearer when we start talking about multiple regression.


:::
::: {.column width = '50%'}

</center>

## Let's Talk Residuals 

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width = '50%'}

At a conference in the Summer of 2025 I met this gentleman on the right 👉

He talked A LOT about how checking residuals is probably the most important thing to do when you run regression models (even more important than checking regression coefficients!). He is probably right 🤷

A **residual** is the distance between the regression line and a data point. Points with large residuals are not predicted well by a regression, whereas points with small residuals are predicted quite well.


<center> Residuals are important because they let us know how well, or, in most cases, *how poorly* our regression describes the data.  </center>

:::
::: {.column width = '50%'}

![[Dan Schley](https://www.rsm.nl/people/dan-schley/#publications){target='_blank'}, Associate Professor at Erasmus University, Rotterdam, NL](Additional%20files/images/Dan.jpg){width=60%}
